messages.subject: Radar plot with polar coordinates
parts:
Dear all,

I did a field experiment, and measured some fruit variables:
- length
- width
- weight
- pulp weight
- ...

I would like to plot each fruit by means of an 'ideogram', meaning as
a radar plot, where the score for each variable is plotted on an axis.
I thought the coord_polar()-function would be appropriate for this,
since in this way, it is possible to visualise different 'types' of
fruits by different radar forms.

I transformed my dataset to this form (originally, each fruit was one
record):

Fruit Variable Score
1 Length 22
1 Width 16
1 Weight 135
1 Pulp weight 56
...

Subsequently, I used following code:

F<-read.table("fruit.txt",header=T)

P<-ggplot(F,aes(Score,Variable))+geom_point() # conventional point
plot #
P + coord_polar () # each variable is represented by one axis, and
scores are indicated by points #

I would like to connect the different scores for one fruit to
facilitate the interpretation of the figure and to distinguish
different fruit 'types'.
If I use the command:

P + coord_polar() + geom_line()

The lines on the polar plot are not straight (due to coordinate
conversion), but I would like straight lines.
Of course, I could use the 'stars' package, but I want to classify the
fruits on harvest location and/or season of harvesting.

Does anybody know how to produce straight lines between the different
scores in the polar plot?

Thanks!
Sebastiaan

radarplots (where I can add grouping variables, change the
linetype, ...)?

Thanks,
Sebastiaan

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: Radar plot with polar coordinates
parts:
On Fri, Dec 4, 2009 at 10:02, Sebastiaan De Smedt
<sebped...@gmail.com> wrote:
> And is there a way to plot a curve in cartesian coordinates that,
> after transformation to polar coordinates, becomes a straight line?
> I've tried to find this for a while but I think my mathematical skills
> are just not good enough, :)
>
> If there is such a transformation, it is possible to write a function
> that generates the data and plots the lines.

I would do the contrary for now: plot the stars in cardinal space. In
that case, the conversions only involve cos/sin: you decide of an
angle, a, for each variable and then use cos(a)*value for the x
coordinate and sin(a)*value for the y coordinate (to be checked, it is
late ;) ). But of course you won't have the nice polar grid behind
everything...

Another way would be to make a rose diagram (Polar Area Pie Chart on
wikipedia): use geom_bar and with your data as weights, in polar
coords. If you fill the bars you should get something that is
perceptually close to the stars you wanted at first.

JiHO
